title: Ardas in grief
hook: the Ardas for the dead asks peace for the one who has gone, and for those left, the strength to accept the Will

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaaraj: name the task, do your part, and ask that it come to a good end. Today, the hardest door the Ardas walks through. Go gently.

A family stands in a gurdwara a few days after a funeral. Some of them haven't slept. Someone holds a framed photo; someone else holds a toddler who doesn't understand why everyone is so quiet. In the days since the death, the Guru Granth Sahib has been read, perhaps from beginning to end. Now the reading is finished. The congregation rises, and the Ardas begins. Somewhere in it, the name of the one who died is spoken aloud, for the last time in this way.
screen: `A FAMILY, A FEW DAYS AFTER.` → `THE READING IS FINISHED.` → `THE NAME IS SPOKEN ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Sikhs usually cremate their dead, and Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns, is sung at the cremation. Over the following days, families often hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, and when it ends, an Ardas is said that is often called the antim ardas, the final prayer. It asks two things. For the one who has gone: that their soul find rest, a place at the Guru's feet, union with the One. And for the ones left: the strength to accept the Will. That word, will, is bhaana, and it runs all through Sikh teaching. Bhaana mannan, accepting the Will, is honored, and it is hard. Guru Arjan put it in a single line. In Raag Asa, on ang 394, he says, in effect: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. An honest note. Accepting the Will doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing and ritual displays of mourning, and treats death as part of the One's order rather than a punishment. But it doesn't forbid tears. Acceptance is something people grow into, sometimes over years, and the Ardas doesn't demand it be finished by Sunday; it asks for the strength to keep moving toward it. And the family isn't asked to do this alone. The whole congregation stands with them, and the line rising spirits, good for all, is said even here.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA AT THE CREMATION.` · `REST FOR THE ONE WHO HAS GONE.` · `BHAANA: THE WILL.` · `ACCEPTANCE TAKES TIME.` · then, large: `IN HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Take this at whatever depth feels right today: bring to mind someone you miss, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, or someone who isn't gone but is far away, and if it hurts, let it hurt a little. Breathe. If you pray, you can ask peace for them, and the strength to accept what you can't change, with a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply wish them peace.
Bhaana, the Will of the One: after a death, the Ardas asks rest for the one who has gone, and for the family, the strength to accept it.
Your line: in his will. Acceptance can take years, and tears are allowed along the way. That's day six hundred forty-one.

chat.says: At the Sikh funeral they prayed to accept the Will. Does that mean no crying?
options: No, tears aren't forbidden. Accepting the Will is something people grow into, sometimes over years.
Yes: accepting the Will means the grief should be finished by the end of the service.
It means asking, in that final prayer, for the loss somehow to be undone.
